name: William the Conqueror
role: Duke of Normandy (1035–1087) and King of England (1066–1087)
summary: A medieval ruler who took England by conquest and governed it through personal oaths of loyalty, a new Norman landholding class and close control of the church. Little survives in his own words; his positions appear mainly in acts he ordered, such as the Domesday survey, the harrying of the north, the oath at Salisbury and the laws issued in his name.

property-fundamental.rationale: Mixed record: Law 7 confirms Edward's law over lands and possessions, but Stenton describes the confiscation of English estates and their transfer to Norman holders, and the Chronicle reports that his stewards took land 'by right and by unright'.

reviewHistory.rationale: Mixed record: Law 7 confirms Edward's law over lands and possessions, but he confiscated the lands of Harold's family and of English resisters and transferred them to followers; the Chronicle says his stewards took land 'by right and by unright'.

conscription.rationale: Stenton reports that he called out the English fyrd, the national levy, against Exeter in 1068 and for the 1072 Scotland expedition, and the Chronicle says the 1073 Maine army was English and French.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Chronicle records that he won Maine in 1073 and, in its obituary, that he held Wales and Anglesey, subdued Scotland and would have taken Ireland, and Stenton describes his 1072 expedition into Scotland; his reign is a record of expansion beyond England and Normandy.

reviewHistory.rationale: He conquered England in 1066 and fought to take Maine (1062-64), invaded Brittany (1064), invaded Scotland (1072) and visited Wales with an army (1081); his reign is a record of expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Law 2 of the laws issued in consultation with his magnates required every freeman to swear loyalty to him, and in 1086 all landholders of account swore oaths of allegiance to him at Sarum; he organised his kingdom as a chain of personal oaths and landholding.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His laws gave Normans a special peace and a murder fine levied on the hundred (Law 3) and set different proof rules for English and French accusers (Law 6).

head-commands-forces.rationale: The Chronicle reports that he himself led armies over the sea to Maine in 1073 and into France in 1087, and Stenton reports that he set out for Scotland in person in 1072.

reviewHistory.rationale: He personally led his armies, from Hastings to the north campaign, and himself named sheriffs, earls, bishops and deputies; his half-brother and wife governed in his absence at his appointment.

reviewHistory.rationale: Law 10 attributed to him forbids killing or hanging for any offence and substitutes blinding and castration, but contested evidence points the other way: the Earl Waltheof was executed in 1076, and the laws' attribution is disputed.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Mixed record: at Lillebonne in 1080 he took jurisdiction over the clergy's grosser offences, the Chronicle says he removed bishops and abbots from their sees, and Stenton reports he rejected the pope's demand for fealty; yet he left English church leaders to carry out their own reforms.

reviewHistory.rationale: Mixed record: he appointed the Norman bishops and abbots, deposed Stigand and other native prelates, was confirmed in ultimate authority over the Norman church at Lillebonne (1080), raided monastic wealth in 1070 and refused a papal request to do fealty; yet he endowed many monasteries and worked with papal legates.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Stenton describes thousands of cases in which an English landowner is replaced in Domesday by a Norman successor, estates he granted to his followers from abroad.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Stenton reports he crushed the 1075 revolt, imprisoned Earl Roger and had Waltheof beheaded, and devastated the north after its revolt; the Chronicle says he imprisoned Odo and that no man dared act against his will.

reviewHistory.rationale: He crushed the revolts of 1068-71 and 1075, imprisoned Earl Roger and Odo of Bayeux, and had Waltheof executed; the Chronicle says no man dared act against his will and credits him with a strict peace.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Mixed record: he issued laws in consultation with his magnates, kept the hundred and shire courts and Edward's law (Laws 7 and 8), but the Chronicle says unlawful exactions grew and 'the more men spake about right law, the more unlawfully they acted'.

notes: Sources are chronicles written after or around events (medium at most); the 'Laws of William' text is a collection of articles whose attribution and date are debated. The Harrying of the North's scale is disputed among historians.  Later pass (2026-11-16): Wikipedia answers re-sourced to Stenton, Freeman, the Chronicle and the Laws; Searched Stenton, Freeman and the Chronicle on law, church, land, war, succession, military levy, slavery and the forest; no stated positions of his own survive on the remaining themes (economy, society, ecology, technology, globalism), so those stay null.
